title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
author: Arthur Conan Doyle
ru: Шерлок Холмс и доктор Ватсон разгадывают тайну страшной собаки, которая преследует род Баскервилей на болотах Девона

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Walking Stick
chapters.text:
Sherlock Holmes was sitting at the breakfast table with his back to me. I was standing by the fire, holding a walking stick that a visitor had left in our Baker Street rooms the night before.

“Well, Watson, what do you make of it?” Holmes asked, without turning round.

“How did you know what I was doing? I believe you have eyes in the back of your head.”

“No, but I have a well-polished silver coffee pot in front of me,” he said. “Come, what can his stick tell us about our visitor?”

It was a fine, heavy stick with a round head. Under the head was a silver band with the words: To James Mortimer, M.R.C.S., from his friends of the C.C.H., 1884.

“He's an older doctor, well respected — his friends gave him this present,” I began. “He's a country doctor who visits his patients on foot — the end is badly worn. And C.C.H. is probably the local hunt — a club of gentlemen who ride after foxes.”

“Really, Watson, you are excellent,” said Holmes. He studied the stick with his magnifying glass. “I'm afraid most of your ideas are wrong. But your mistakes help me to find the truth. C.C.H. must be Charing Cross Hospital. Friends give a present like this when a man leaves, so he worked there and then moved to the country. A successful doctor doesn't leave London for a country village, so he was young — under thirty, friendly, not ambitious, a little absent-minded. And he owns a dog that is larger than a terrier and smaller than a mastiff.”

I laughed. “How can you possibly know about the dog?”

“The dog carries the stick for its master — see the marks of its teeth? Too far apart for a terrier, too close for a mastiff. It might be—” He went to the window. “Yes. A curly-haired spaniel. He's on our doorstep now, with his master.”

A moment later a tall, thin man came in. He had a long nose like a bird's beak and kind grey eyes behind gold glasses. A little brown spaniel ran in at his feet.

“My stick!” he cried happily. “I wouldn't lose it for the world.”

“A present from Charing Cross Hospital?” asked Holmes.

“Yes, when I got married and left London. I'm Dr Mortimer, from Grimpen, on Dartmoor, in Devon.” He looked at Holmes's head with great interest. “What a wonderful skull you have, sir! But I haven't come about skulls. I've come because you are the second best expert on crime in Europe.”

“Indeed? And who is the first?” Holmes asked coldly.

“Monsieur Bertillon, in France. But for a practical man, sir, there's nobody like you.” Dr Mortimer took an old paper from his pocket. “This was written in 1742. It tells the story of the Baskerville family — and of the hound.”

He began to read. Long ago, it said, Baskerville Hall belonged to Hugo Baskerville, a wild and cruel man. One night he and his friends carried off a farmer's daughter and locked her in a room upstairs. While the men were drinking below, the girl climbed down the ivy and ran away across the moor — the wide, wild land of grass, rock and bog around the Hall.

When Hugo found the room empty, he swore he would give his body and soul to the Devil if he could only catch her. He let his dogs loose and rode after her into the night. His friends followed. Under the moon they found the girl dead of fear, and Hugo lying near her. Standing over him was a great black beast, shaped like a hound, but larger than any hound on earth. As they watched, it tore out Hugo's throat and turned its burning eyes on them.

“So, my sons,” the paper ended, “do not cross the moor in those dark hours when the powers of evil are strong.”

Holmes yawned. “Interesting — to a collector of fairy tales.”

Dr Mortimer took a newspaper from his pocket. “Then let me read you something more modern, Mr Holmes. Three months ago, Sir Charles Baskerville died. And I'm not sure that the hound is a fairy tale at all.”

chapters.title: Chapter 2. Footprints in the Yew Alley
chapters.text:
The report in the newspaper was short. Sir Charles Baskerville had made a fortune in South Africa and come home to Baskerville Hall two years before. He was a kind, generous man, and he spent much of his money helping his poorer neighbours. He lived simply, with only two servants: Barrymore, the butler, and his wife, the housekeeper.

Sir Charles had a weak heart. Every night before bed he liked to walk along the Yew Alley — a long garden path between two high, dark walls of yew trees. Halfway along there was a small gate that opened onto the moor.

On the night of the fourth of May he went out for his walk as usual, smoking a cigar. He never came back. At midnight Barrymore found the front door still open. He took a lamp and went to look for his master, and he found him at the end of the alley, lying on his face, dead.

There were no marks of violence on the body. However, Sir Charles's face was so strangely twisted that Dr Mortimer could hardly recognize his old friend. The cause of death was his heart. The next heir was his nephew, Sir Henry Baskerville, who was now on his way home from Canada.

“Those are the public facts,” said Holmes, putting his fingertips together. “Now tell me the private ones.”

Dr Mortimer looked uncomfortable. “I haven't told anyone. A man of science doesn't want people to think that he believes in ghosts.” He took a deep breath. “Sir Charles believed the legend completely. He would never go out on the moor at night. He often asked me if I had ever seen a strange animal there, or heard a dog howling.

“About three weeks before he died, I drove up to the Hall one evening. Sir Charles was standing at the door. Suddenly he stared past me with a look of terrible fear. I turned, and I just saw something cross the end of the drive. It looked like a large black calf. I went after it, but it had gone. The poor man was shaking. After that night I told him to go to London for a few months, for the sake of his heart. He had decided to go. And then...”

“Go on.”

“I was the first doctor there that night. Sir Charles had stood for some minutes by the gate to the moor — there was ash from his cigar on the ground. Then he walked on down the alley, past the gate, and his footprints changed. Barrymore said that he seemed to be walking on his toes.”

Holmes's eyes were shining now. “And the ground around the body?”

“Barrymore said there were no other footprints. But he didn't look carefully. I did. Some distance from the body there were fresh, clear prints.”

“A man's or a woman's?”

Dr Mortimer looked at us strangely for a moment. Then his voice dropped almost to a whisper.

“Mr Holmes, they were the footprints of a gigantic hound!”

chapters.title: Chapter 3. A Warning for Sir Henry
chapters.text:
For a moment nobody spoke. I felt a cold shiver run down my back, and even Holmes leaned forward in his chair.

“You saw this yourself?”

“As clearly as I see you.”

“And you said nothing?”

“What was the use?”

Holmes fired questions at him. How far from the body were the prints? About twenty yards. Did they come any closer? No. Could a dog get through the yew hedges? Impossible — they were twelve feet high, and the only way out to the moor was through the gate.

“And after he left the gate,” said Holmes slowly, “Sir Charles was not walking on his toes, Dr Mortimer. He was running. Running desperately for his life, until his heart burst and he fell on his face. And before that he waited at the gate for several minutes. An old man who was afraid of the moor, standing at that gate in the dark? No. He was waiting for someone.”

Dr Mortimer looked at his watch. “Sir Henry arrives at Waterloo station in an hour, Mr Holmes. Every Baskerville who lives at the Hall seems to meet a terrible end. Should I take him there?”

“Bring him here tomorrow at ten o'clock,” said Holmes. “And say nothing to him until then.”

All that day Holmes sat in his armchair, smoking pipe after pipe. When I came home in the evening, the room was so full of smoke that I could hardly see the lamp.

“I've been to Devon,” he said.

“In spirit?”

“Exactly.” He showed me a large map of Dartmoor. “Here is Baskerville Hall. Here is the village of Grimpen, where Dr Mortimer lives. Here, Merripit House — the home of a naturalist called Stapleton, a man who studies plants and insects. Here, fourteen miles away, is the great prison at Princetown. And all around them, the empty moor. A perfect stage for the Devil, if he wants to play a part in this.”

At ten the next morning, Sir Henry Baskerville arrived with Dr Mortimer. He was a small, strong man of about thirty, with a dark, determined face. Years of farming in Canada had made his skin brown.

“Something strange has happened already, Mr Holmes,” he said. “This came to my hotel this morning.”

He put an envelope on the table. Inside was a single sheet of paper. Words cut out of a newspaper were stuck on it:

As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.

Only the word “moor” was written by hand, in ink.

“Now, who knew that I was staying at the Northumberland Hotel?” said Sir Henry. “I only chose it last night.”

Holmes held the paper to the light. “These words were cut from yesterday's Times, from an article about trade. Someone cut them out with small nail scissors. And the address was written in a hotel. The pen made two blots in one short word, and it ran out of ink three times in the short address. Hotel pens and ink are always bad.”

“Wonderful,” said Sir Henry. “Is there anything you can't tell from a piece of paper?”

“Has anything else happened to you in London?”

Sir Henry laughed. “Only that somebody stole one of my boots. One of my new brown boots — I've never even worn them. I put the pair outside my door last night for cleaning, and this morning there was only one.”

Then Dr Mortimer told him the legend and the full story of his uncle's death. Sir Henry listened in silence. At the end he struck the table with his fist.

“There's no devil in hell, Mr Holmes, and no man on earth, who can stop me from going to the home of my own people.”

He and Dr Mortimer left to walk back to the hotel. The moment the door closed, Holmes changed completely.

“Your hat and boots, Watson, quick! There isn't a moment to lose!”

chapters.title: Chapter 4. The Man with the Black Beard
chapters.text:
We ran down the stairs and into the street. Two hundred yards ahead of us we could see Sir Henry and Dr Mortimer walking towards Oxford Street.

“Slowly now,” said Holmes. “We don't want them to see us. Someone else is following them, and I want to see him.”

We walked behind them for some time. Suddenly Holmes gave a little cry. A cab — a small carriage pulled by one horse — had stopped on the other side of the street. Now it was moving slowly behind our two friends. In the window I saw a man with a thick black beard and sharp, bright eyes. The next moment he saw us too. He shouted something to the driver, and the cab flew off down Regent Street.

Holmes ran after it, but it was no use. He came back red in the face.

“What bad luck, and what bad management! If you write about this case, Watson, you must put this down against me. But at least I have the number of the cab: 2704.”

At two o'clock we went to Sir Henry's hotel. We found him on the stairs, red with anger, with an old black boot in his hand.

“They're playing games with me, Mr Holmes! First they take one new brown boot, and now one of my old black ones has gone too!”

The brown boot was found later that afternoon, under a cupboard in his room, although the hotel staff swore they had looked there before. Holmes said nothing, but I could see that he was thinking hard.

“Dr Mortimer,” he asked, “who lives at Baskerville Hall now?”

“Only the Barrymores.”

“Has Barrymore got a beard?”

“Yes. A full black beard.”

Holmes sent a telegram — a short message by telegraph — to Barrymore at once: Is everything ready for Sir Henry? It was to be given into Barrymore's own hand. That way we would know if he was really in Devon.

“Sir Henry,” said Holmes, “you must not go to the Hall alone. I can't come myself — an important case is keeping me in London. But my friend Watson is the best man I know to stand beside you in danger.”

I was surprised, but Sir Henry shook my hand warmly. So it was settled: we would travel to Devon on Saturday.

That evening two answers came. The first was the reply to the telegram: Barrymore was at the Hall. The second was a knock on our door. A rough-looking man came in, turning his hat in his hands. He was John Clayton, the driver of cab number 2704.

“A gentleman took my cab this morning,” he said. “He told me he was a detective and paid me two guineas — good money — to do what he said all day. First we went to the Northumberland Hotel and waited. Then we followed two gentlemen, until he suddenly shouted at me to drive fast to Waterloo station. He got out there.”

“What did he look like?” asked Holmes.

“About forty, I'd say. Not tall. Dressed like a gentleman, with a black beard, cut square, and a pale face.”

“Did he tell you his name?”

“Yes, sir. As he got out, he told me. His name was Mr Sherlock Holmes.”

For a moment Holmes stared. Then he burst out laughing.

“He's beaten us this time, Watson! He's a clever one, this man.” But when the cabman had gone, he was serious again. “I don't like sending you down there, Watson. It's an ugly business, a dangerous business. And the more I see of it, the less I like it.”

chapters.title: Chapter 5. Baskerville Hall
chapters.text:
Holmes came with us to Paddington station on Saturday morning.

“Send me facts, Watson, only facts,” he said. “Watch everyone near Sir Henry: the Barrymores, Dr Mortimer, Mr Stapleton the naturalist and his sister — a young and attractive lady, I hear. And keep your revolver with you, night and day.” Then he turned to Sir Henry. “And remember the old story, Sir Henry. Never go out on the moor alone at night, when the powers of evil are strong.”

It was a long journey. Sir Henry sat with his face at the window, as excited as a boy. He laughed with pleasure at the red earth of Devon and the green fields and the little farms.

At the small country station a carriage was waiting for us. There were soldiers on the platform, and as we drove away, I saw another soldier on horseback, on a hill above the road, with his rifle ready.

“Is something wrong?” Dr Mortimer asked the driver.

“A prisoner has escaped from Princetown, sir. Three days ago now. His name's Selden — the murderer. He's out on the moor somewhere, and folks round here are scared.”

Soon the fields were behind us, and the moor rose all around: brown and grey hills, cold and empty, with strange piles of broken rock on their tops. People here call them tors. A cold wind blew across the land. Sir Henry stopped laughing and pulled his coat closer around him.

At last we turned in through iron gates. A long, dark avenue of old trees led to the house. Baskerville Hall stood at the end of it: a heavy old building with two black towers, its walls covered in ivy.

“I don't wonder my uncle felt nervous,” said Sir Henry quietly. “It's enough to frighten anyone. I'll have electric lights all along here in six months.”

Barrymore was waiting at the door — a tall, handsome man with a square black beard and a pale face. He showed us inside. The hall was dark, with heavy wooden beams and the heads of deer on the walls. In the dining room, the faces of Baskervilles from long ago looked down at us from their portraits. Nobody felt like talking much at dinner.

After the meal Barrymore spoke to Sir Henry. “My wife and I will be leaving you soon, sir, when you have new servants. We were very attached to Sir Charles. His death has shocked us, and the Hall will never be the same for us.”

That night I could not sleep. From my window I could see the moor, lying cold and silent under the moon, and I could hear the wind moaning in the trees. The clock struck one, then two.

And then, in the silence of the night, I heard a sound — clear and close, and impossible to mistake. It was a woman crying: the deep, broken sobs of someone with a terrible sorrow.

The sound was coming from somewhere inside the house.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. The Naturalist and His Sister
chapters.text:
At breakfast the next morning, Sir Henry said that he had heard the crying too. He called Barrymore.

The butler's pale face went even paler. “There are only two women in the house, Sir Henry. The kitchen maid sleeps in the other wing. And my wife — I can tell you that the sound did not come from her.”

But he was lying. An hour later I met Mrs Barrymore in the long corridor, with the sun on her face. She was a large, serious woman, and her eyes were red and swollen. It was she who had cried in the night. And if Barrymore had lied about that, what else was he hiding?

I walked four miles to the post office at Grimpen to ask about Holmes's telegram.

“Yes, sir,” said the postmaster. “My boy took it up to the Hall. He gave it to Mrs Barrymore. Mr Barrymore was up in the attic, she said.”

So nobody had actually seen Barrymore at the Hall that day. He could have been in London, wearing his black beard and riding in a cab.

I was walking back across the moor, deep in thought, when I heard someone running behind me. A small, thin, clean-shaven man with fair hair was hurrying towards me. He had a green butterfly net in his hand.

“Excuse me, Dr Watson,” he said, a little out of breath. “Dr Mortimer told me about you. I'm Stapleton, from Merripit House. Has Mr Sherlock Holmes come down to Devon too?”

“No, he's busy in London.”

“What a pity.” He walked along beside me, talking happily about the moor. Then he stopped and pointed to a wide, flat plain below us. Here and there it was bright green, much brighter than the land around it.

“That's the great Grimpen Mire,” he said. “A bog — wet, soft ground with no bottom. One false step there means death for a man or an animal. Look!”

Something brown was moving among the green grass. Then a long neck rose up, and a terrible cry rang across the moor. It was a moor pony, sinking into the mud. It fought and screamed, but slowly the mire pulled it down, until only its head was showing. Then that too was gone.

“That's the second in two days,” said Stapleton calmly. “But I know the way to its centre, where there are rare plants and butterflies.”

At that moment a long, low howl rose from the moor. It filled the whole air, deep and sad and wild, then slowly died away.

“What on earth was that?” I asked.

Stapleton looked at me with a strange expression. “The farmers say it's the Hound of the Baskervilles calling for its prey. But I think it's a bird — a bittern, perhaps.”

Suddenly he saw a butterfly, and he was off, jumping from one dry spot to another after it. A moment later, I heard quick steps. A woman was coming towards me along the path. She was tall and beautiful, with dark hair and dark eyes — very unlike her fair-haired brother.

Her face was white. “Go back!” she said quickly. “Go straight back to London, at once!”

“But why?”

“I can't explain. But for God's sake, do what I say. Never come near the moor again.” Then she saw her brother returning. “Quiet,” she whispered. “Not a word about this.”

Stapleton came up, his net over his shoulder. “Hello, Beryl! I see you two have already met.”

“Yes. I was telling Sir Henry that it's too late in the year for the orchids.”

“Sir Henry?” Stapleton said slowly. “But this is Dr Watson, his friend.”

Her face turned red. Stapleton looked at her, then at me, and something hard came into his eyes. It was there for only a second.

But I knew that the warning had not been meant for me. It had been meant for Sir Henry. And Miss Stapleton was afraid — terribly afraid — of something.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. A Light in the Window
chapters.text:
In the weeks that followed, I wrote long letters to Holmes in London. There was a lot to report.

The first news was simple: Sir Henry had fallen in love with Beryl Stapleton. That was no surprise — she was a beautiful woman, and life at the Hall was lonely. The surprise was her brother. You might think that Stapleton would be glad to see his sister marry a rich baronet — a gentleman with a title. But whenever Sir Henry and Beryl were together, Stapleton was never far away, watching them with a cold, hard face.

One day Sir Henry put on his hat to go out alone.

“Holmes said you mustn't go out on the moor alone,” I reminded him.

He laughed and put his hand on my shoulder. “My dear fellow, even Holmes can't expect me to take a friend with me when I go to see a lady.”

I let him go, and then I was sorry. I followed him, and from a hill I saw him walking with Miss Stapleton on the path below. He took her in his arms. She seemed to be trying to pull away. And then Stapleton came running across the moor towards them, waving his net, red with anger. He shouted at Sir Henry, then took his sister by the arm and marched her away.

“What's wrong with me, Watson?” Sir Henry asked me later, hurt and confused. “Am I not good enough for her? He wouldn't even let me finish speaking!”

The next day Stapleton came to the Hall to apologise. “She's all I have in the world,” he said. “I was afraid of losing her. Please forgive me. If you'll wait three months, Sir Henry, and just be her friend until then, I won't stand in your way.”

It was very strange. But I had another mystery to think about.

One night, at about two o'clock, I heard soft footsteps outside my door. I looked out. Barrymore was walking slowly down the corridor in his shirt and trousers, with a candle in his hand. He went into an empty bedroom at the end. Through the open door I saw him standing at the window, holding the candle against the glass and staring out into the black night. After a few minutes he gave a deep groan, put out the light and went back to his room.

I told Sir Henry everything, and we decided to wait for him. For two nights nothing happened. On the third night, at two in the morning, we heard the footsteps. We followed quietly and found Barrymore at the window with his candle, exactly as before.

“What are you doing here, Barrymore?” said Sir Henry.

The butler jumped. His face was white and his hand was shaking so much that the candle danced. “Nothing, sir. I was just checking that the window was closed.”

“Don't lie to me. Tell me the truth!”

“It isn't my secret, sir. I can't tell you.”

I took the candle from his hand and held it to the window, as he had done. Far away, on the black moor, a tiny point of yellow light was burning. I moved the candle across the window. The distant light moved too.

“It's a signal!” I cried. “Somebody out there is answering. Who is it, Barrymore?”

Before he could reply, there was a step at the door. Mrs Barrymore stood there, even paler than her husband.

“Don't blame him, Sir Henry,” she said. “He did it for me. The man out there on the moor is my brother. He's Selden — the escaped prisoner.”

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The Man on the Tor
chapters.text:
Mrs Barrymore told us everything. Selden was her younger brother. Their mother had spoiled him as a boy, and when he grew up he fell into bad company. He went from bad to worse, until at last he killed a man. But to her he was still the little curly-haired boy she had played with as a child.

“When he escaped, he came here, sir, because he knew I would help him. He was starving. Every night we put a light in the window to see if he's still there. If he answers, my husband takes him some bread and meat. That's all. We're honest people, sir — whatever he's done, I couldn't let him die.”

Sir Henry sent them back to bed. Then he turned to me.

“That man is a murderer, Watson. He's hiding out there near the Stapletons' house, and nobody's safe while he's free. I'm going to catch him tonight.”

I fetched my revolver, and five minutes later we were out on the moor. It was a dark night with a cold wind, and the light still burned on the hill in front of us. We walked fast, stumbling over rocks and rough grass.

Suddenly, out of the darkness, came that strange sound — the long, deep howl I had heard on the day I met Stapleton. It rose louder and louder, and then it slowly sank away into silence.

Sir Henry grabbed my arm. Even in the dark I could see that his face was white.

“Watson, what's that?”

“I don't know. The people here say it's... the Hound.”

He was quiet for a moment. “I'm not a coward, Watson,” he said at last, “but that sound froze my blood. Can there be some truth in the old story?” Then he took a deep breath. “No. We've come to catch this man, and we'll do it, even if all the devils of hell are loose on the moor.”

We went on. The light was coming from a candle pushed into a crack in the rocks, so that nobody could see it except from the Hall. We were creeping towards it when a terrible face rose up over the rocks — a dirty, wild face with a rough beard and small, cunning eyes, like an animal's. It was Selden. He saw us, gave a shout and threw a stone, which broke on the rock beside us. Then he was gone, running down the hill.

We chased him across the moor, but he was too fast for us. Soon we stopped, out of breath, and sat down on a rock. The moon was rising now on our right, silver and huge.

And then I saw him.

On the top of a tor, black against the bright moon, stood the figure of a man. He was tall and thin. He stood quite still, with his arms folded and his head bent, like a statue, looking down over the wide dark moor. It was not Selden — he had run off in the other direction. This was somebody else.

I turned to show Sir Henry. But when I looked back, the top of the tor was empty. The man had vanished.

chapters.title: Chapter 9. The Stone Hut
chapters.text:
The next morning Barrymore asked to speak to Sir Henry.

“My wife's brother is leaving for South America in a few days, sir. Please don't tell the police. And in return, I'll tell you something that I've kept secret for too long. It's about Sir Charles.”

On the morning of his death, Barrymore said, Sir Charles had received a letter from the town of Coombe Tracey, in a woman's handwriting. Some weeks later Mrs Barrymore was cleaning his study and found ashes of burnt paper in the fireplace. One small piece had not burned. On it were the words: Please, please, as you are a gentleman, burn this letter, and be at the gate by ten o'clock. It was signed with two letters: L.L.

Dr Mortimer helped us find her. Laura Lyons lived in Coombe Tracey. Her husband had left her, and she earned a little money by typing letters for people. Sir Charles had helped her — and so had Mr Stapleton.

I drove to Coombe Tracey the same afternoon. Mrs Lyons was a very pretty woman with hazel eyes. When I mentioned the letter, her face went pale.

“Yes, I wrote it,” she said at last. “I needed money to free myself from my husband. Sir Charles was kind and generous, so I asked him to meet me. But I never went. Somebody else helped me first.”

“Why ask him to meet you at night, at a gate in his garden?”

“He was leaving for London the next day.”

I didn't believe her. She was telling the truth about some things, but she was hiding something. I left feeling angry and confused.

On my way home I passed the house of old Mr Frankland, a bad-tempered neighbour who loved arguments. He had a telescope on his roof, and he called me in to look through it.

“There!” he cried. “Do you see that boy with a bundle? Every day he crosses the moor at the same time. He's taking food to that prisoner, mark my words!”

But I knew better. Selden got his food from the Barrymores. The boy was carrying it to somebody else — to the man I had seen on the tor.

I went after him at once. On the side of the hill I found a circle of old stone huts, built by people who had lived on the moor thousands of years ago. Only one still had a roof. I crept up to it with my revolver in my hand. It was empty.

Somebody was living there. There was a blanket on the stone floor, a cooking pot, some tins of food, a loaf of bread and a jug of water. On a flat stone lay a piece of paper. I picked it up and read:

Dr Watson has gone to Coombe Tracey.

A cold feeling went through me. This man was not following Sir Henry. He was following me.

I decided to wait for him. I sat in the darkest corner of the hut with my revolver ready, and I watched the sun go down over the moor. Then, at last, I heard boots striking on stone. They came closer and closer. A shadow fell across the doorway.

“It's a lovely evening, my dear Watson,” said a well-known voice. “I really think you'll be more comfortable outside than in.”

chapters.title: Chapter 10. Death on the Moor
chapters.text:
I came out of the hut, hardly able to believe my eyes. There on a stone sat Sherlock Holmes, thin and brown from the sun, as calm as if he were in Baker Street.

“Holmes! You've been here all the time? And I thought you were in London!”

“If I had stayed at the Hall with you, our enemy would have been careful. Out here I could watch him without being seen. Young Cartwright — the boy with the bundle — brought me food from the village, and your letters were sent on to me. They were excellent, Watson.”

I was hurt, but I was so glad to see him that I soon forgot it. I told him about Laura Lyons.

“That fills a gap,” said Holmes. “You see, Mrs Lyons and Stapleton are very close friends. And Stapleton is our man, Watson. And the lady you know as Miss Stapleton is not his sister at all. She's his wife.”

“His wife! But why—”

“A beautiful unmarried sister was a useful trap for Sir Henry. And as a single man, he could promise to marry Laura Lyons — she believes him even now. But I don't have enough proof yet. I need one more day. Then—”

A terrible scream broke the silence of the moor — a long scream of horror and pain. After it came another sound, which made my blood turn cold: a deep, low growl, and then nothing.

“The hound!” cried Holmes. “Come, Watson! Quick! We may be too late!”

We ran over the dark moor, stumbling over rocks. At the bottom of a steep, rocky slope we found a body lying face down. I knew the clothes at once: a red-brown tweed suit. It was the suit Sir Henry had worn on the morning when he came to Baker Street.

“Watson,” said Holmes in a broken voice, “I'll never forgive myself.”

I lit a match and we turned the body over. Then Holmes gave a shout and danced like a madman in the dark.

“A beard! A beard! It isn't Sir Henry — it's the prisoner!”

It was Selden. Barrymore had given him some of Sir Henry's old clothes. And the hound had been trained to follow Sir Henry's smell.

“That's why the boot was stolen in London,” said Holmes. “The new one was no use — it had never been worn. Stapleton needed an old boot with Sir Henry's smell on it.”

At that moment we saw the red end of a cigar coming towards us. It was Stapleton. When he saw the body, he stopped.

“Dr Watson! Who... is it Sir Henry?”

“No. It's Selden, the escaped prisoner.”

For a second his face showed something like disappointment. Then he looked from me to Holmes. “What a terrible thing. Did you hear anything? A... dog, perhaps?”

“No,” said Holmes calmly. “He must have fallen from the rocks.”

Stapleton said goodnight and walked away into the dark.

Later that evening Holmes came back with me to the Hall. After dinner he looked for a long time at the old family portraits. He stopped in front of one: a man in a black velvet coat, with a wide hat and long curls.

“Is that Hugo Baskerville, who started all the trouble?” he asked.

“Yes,” said Sir Henry.

Holmes climbed onto a chair. With his arm, he covered the hat and the long hair.

“Good heavens!” I cried.

The face of Stapleton was looking out of the picture.

“He's a Baskerville,” said Holmes. “That explains everything. If Sir Henry dies, the Hall and the money will be his.” Then he laughed, which he did very rarely. “We have him, Watson! Tomorrow night he'll be caught in our net, like one of his own butterflies.”

chapters.title: Chapter 11. The Hound of the Baskervilles
chapters.text:
The next morning Holmes gave Sir Henry some strange orders. Holmes and I would take the train to London. Sir Henry would go to dinner at Merripit House that evening, and then walk home across the moor — alone.

“Trust me,” said Holmes. “Go straight along the path, and don't turn off it.”

Sir Henry was hurt, but he agreed. We did not go to London. At the station we met Inspector Lestrade, a small, tough detective from Scotland Yard. Then we drove to Coombe Tracey and showed Laura Lyons an old photograph of the Stapletons as husband and wife. When she saw that Stapleton had lied to her, she told us the truth: he had made her write to Sir Charles — and then stopped her from going.

That night, the three of us hid among the rocks near Merripit House. Through the window we could see Sir Henry and Stapleton smoking after dinner. Once Stapleton went out to a small shed behind the house. We heard a strange noise inside it, and then he came back.

Now something white was coming across the moor towards us: fog from the Grimpen Mire. It moved slowly, like a thick, silent wall.

“This is bad,” said Holmes. “If Sir Henry isn't out in a quarter of an hour, we won't be able to see the path.”

At last the door opened and Sir Henry came out. He walked quickly past us. And then we heard it — the quick, soft sound of running feet, somewhere in the fog.

Out of the white wall jumped a hound. It was an enormous coal-black dog, but not a dog that any human eye had ever seen. Fire came out of its open mouth. Its eyes glowed. Its head and neck were outlined in flickering flame. Lestrade screamed and fell on his face.

Holmes and I fired together. The creature gave a terrible howl — it was hurt. If it could be hurt, it could be killed! But it did not stop. It jumped on Sir Henry and knocked him down. Holmes ran faster than I had ever seen a man run and emptied his revolver into the creature's side. With a last howl, it rolled over and lay still.

Sir Henry had fainted, but he was alive. The dog was as big as a small lion, half bloodhound and half mastiff. Holmes touched its mouth, and his fingers shone in the dark.

“Phosphorus,” he said. “A chemical that glows. A clever trick — it made the dog look like the devil himself.”

We ran to Merripit House. Stapleton had gone. But in a locked bedroom upstairs we found Beryl Stapleton, tied to a post, with the marks of a whip on her neck.

“Has he escaped?” she asked. “Then he's gone to an old mine on an island in the Mire. That's where he kept the dog.”

In the morning, when the fog had lifted, she showed us the path through the Mire. On the way we found an old black boot: Sir Henry's. Stapleton had used it to teach the hound his smell. But there was no other sign of Stapleton. Somewhere in that soft green mud, the great Grimpen Mire had swallowed him for ever.

A month later, on a foggy evening in Baker Street, Holmes explained the rest. Stapleton was the son of Sir Charles's younger brother, who had gone to South America. When he learned that only two lives stood between him and a fortune, he came to Devon under a false name. He bought the dog in London. He used Laura Lyons to bring the old man to the gate, and then he let the hound loose. Sir Charles's weak heart did the rest. Beryl had refused to help him with Sir Henry. It was she who had sent the warning made of newspaper words. And the man with the black beard in the cab? Stapleton, of course, in a false beard.

Sir Henry was now travelling around the world with Dr Mortimer, to rest his nerves and heal his broken heart.

“And now, my dear Watson,” said Holmes, “I think we can turn our thoughts to pleasanter things. I have a box at the opera tonight. Could you be ready in half an hour?”
